cards.body: More than 100 genes are linked to autism. So you might expect more than 100 kinds of brain biology. A large mouse study found something simpler. In the front of the brain, gene activity fell into just two opposite patterns. And mice could move from one pattern to the other.
cards.evidence: mouse study · 17 mouse lines · human check: brain tissue from 40 autistic and 17 non-autistic people · published in Scie

sections.text:
Researchers raised 17 kinds of mice side by side. Each kind carried a different gene change linked to autism. The team then measured which genes were switched on, and how strongly, in the prefrontal cortex. That is the front part of the brain, used for planning and social behavior.

Why does this matter? Autism genetics is crowded. Scientists want to sort the genes into a few groups that make biological sense, because each group might one day need its own treatment. Earlier mouse studies usually looked at one gene change, in one brain region, at one age. This study compared all 17 under the same conditions. It included both sexes, different ages and different drug exposures.

The result was two opposite patterns. In the first, genes that help neurons talk to each other were less active than usual. Genes that manage DNA and process RNA (the cell's working copies of genes) were more active. The second pattern was the exact reverse. Very different gene changes seemed to end up in one of the same two places.

But the groups were not fixed. In 7 of the 17 mouse lines, males and females with the same gene change fell into different groups. Some mice switched groups as they grew up. And in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory, the clean split did not appear at all.

So study investigator Eunjoon Kim says it is too early to call these "subtypes." For now, he says, they are best seen as "temporary biological states." Still, one thing strikes him. When mice switch, they move between the same two patterns. No new pattern appears.

The team also checked brain tissue from 40 autistic people and 17 non-autistic people. The autistic samples also split into two roughly opposite patterns, but less clearly. Kim calls the human signal weak. He thinks this may be because the people differed in age, sex and seizure history. More samples, from more brain regions, could confirm the link.

Kaustubh Supekar of Stanford, who was not part of the study, sees a wider lesson. Autism's variety may shift with age and with the part of the body you look at. It may not fall into fixed, permanent types. Most searches for autism subgroups have used brain scans. Molecular data, like these gene readings, could add another view. Combined with genetic, imaging and clinical data, it might one day show subgroups that change over time.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study, mostly in mice. The clean two-pattern split showed up in only one brain region. The human signal was weak and came from a small, mixed set of brain samples.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Many roads, two destinations — but the traveller does not always stay put.

recall.q: What two patterns did the study find, and why won't the researchers call them autism subtypes yet?
recall.a: In one pattern, genes that help neurons communicate were less active and genes for DNA and RNA work were more active; the other pattern was the reverse. They are not called subtypes because they were not fixed: sex and age changed a mouse's group, and the split did not appear in the hippocampus.

cards.title: A frog that hunts by touch, with 64 fingertips per hand
cards.body: The water frog Pipa pipa catches fish without looking and without chasing them. Each hand splits into 64 fingertips. Those fingertips are only 8 percent of the front limb, but they get 34 percent of the brain space that maps it.
cards.evidence: single lab study · high-speed video and brain mapping · sample size not stated

sections.text:
A flat brown frog lies still at the bottom of a muddy river. Its arms are stretched out wide, like a pair of goalposts. A small fish swims between them. In a flash, the frog sucks it into its mouth and swallows it whole. The frog has no tongue. It never chased anything.

This is Pipa pipa. A recent paper from Duncan Leitch's lab at the University of California, Los Angeles, says it hunts by touch, not sight. The team filmed the frogs with high-speed cameras. Even with no help from their eyes, the frogs caught fish that swam near their hands. The fish did not even have to touch them.

Leitch has loved reptiles and amphibians since he was a child. He first met Pipa in old books about strange animals, for a different reason: the mother carries her eggs inside the skin of her back, and fully formed little frogs climb out. Then he watched the frogs hunt at a zoo. That is what brought them into his lab.

The secret is in the hands. Each front limb has four fingers. Each finger splits into four branches, and each branch splits four ways again. That makes 64 very sensitive fingertips per hand. Leitch thinks the frog may be growing its sensing surface, "almost like an antennae."

The brain tells the same story. In frogs, a brain area called the optic tectum does the job of the sensory cortex in mammals: it handles touch and other senses. The fingertips are only 8 percent of the front limb's surface. But they take up 34 percent of the tectum's space for the front limb.

So the team says the fingertips work as a fovea. A fovea is a small patch packed with sensors that gets far more brain space than its size suggests. Your eye has one: a tiny spot in the retina where your vision is sharpest. The star-nosed mole has one in the fleshy star on its nose. Pipa pipa may have built its fovea into its hands.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The fovea idea comes from one lab. It is a proposal, not a settled fact. The report does not say how many frogs were studied. It also does not explain how the fingertips sense a fish that never touches them.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The brain does not give every part of the body equal space. It gives the most space to the parts that matter most.

recall.q: Why do Leitch and his team call the frog's fingertips a fovea?
recall.a: The fingertips are only 8 percent of the front limb's surface, but they take up 34 percent of the brain space that maps it. Like the sharpest spot in the eye, they are packed with sensors and get far more brain space than their size suggests. The frog uses them to catch fish by touch.

cards.title: World rice output may fall 9% as demand rises 14%
cards.body: India will harvest less rice too. But IREF says India has enough stored rice to sell abroad and become a key supplier.

sections.text:
When the world grows less rice but wants more, a gap opens. Someone has to fill it.

India's own harvest is expected to shrink. But IREF says India has large surplus stocks. That means rice kept in storage beyond what the country needs. India can sell this extra rice to other countries.

Other big rice-growing countries are under pressure. This leaves room for Indian exporters. But costs are rising for everyone. Higher fuel and fertilizer prices are still shaking the global rice market.

sections.label: The numbers
items: India's harvest: also expected to fall
India's edge: surplus rice in storage
Reported: 1 October 2026

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: This time, India's strength comes from old stocks, not a big new harvest. If those stocks fill the world's gap, India gains weight in the rice trade.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Fuel and fertilizer costs. They could squeeze India's exporters too.

recall.q: India's own rice harvest is expected to fall. So why does IREF think India can become a key rice supplier?
recall.a: The world is expected to grow 9% less rice while demand rises 14%. India has surplus rice in storage, so it can sell abroad to fill that gap while other big producers are under pressure.
